title: Real-time intravital microscopy of individual nanoparticle dynamics in liver and tumors of live mice
protocol: Anesthetize mouse with 4% isoflurane (21% oxygen, balance nitrogen) until breathing is slow and deep.
Maintain body temperature at 37 °C using a heating pad and/or heat lamp.
Draw 50-100 μl of blood from the orbital sinus or other aseptic draw site using a heparinized microhematocrit tube.
Transfer blood into an EDTA-coated microcentrifuge tube.
Cap the EDTA-coated microcentrifuge tube immediately after drawing blood.
Invert the tube to mix.
Centrifuge the whole blood for 10 min at 270 rcf (2000 rpm).
Pipette off the clear serum layer, being careful not to disturb the red blood cell pellet.
Transfer 15 μl of RBCs into a fresh, uncoated 1.6 ml microcentrifuge tube.
Add 750 μl pre-warmed (37 °C) GPBS.
Add 7.5 μl DiD labeling solution, mix by gently inverting the tube.
Add an additional 750 μl GPBS.
Cover from light and incubate at 37 °C for 15 minutes.
Spin DiD-labeled RBCs for 5 min at 150 rcf (1500 rpm).
Remove the supernatant.
Repeat step 4.
Invert the tube and flick the tip to mix.
Spin DiD-labeled RBCs for 5 min at 150 rcf (1500 rpm).
Wash cells twice in 1000 μl GPBS.
Resuspend cells in 100 μl sterile PBS.
Re-anesthetize mouse using isoflurane.
Inject the DiD-labeled RBCs via retro-orbital route or into the tail vein.
Store RBCs at 4 °C in PBS for up to 1 week.
Anesthetize mouse with 4% isoflurane in an induction chamber until breathing is slow and deep.
Place the mouse on a cotton pad after reaching a surgical level of anesthesia.
Reduce isoflurane concentration to 2%.
Alternatively, anesthetize the mouse by intraperitoneal injection of ketamine/xylazine working solution.
Maintain body temperature at 37 °C using a heating pad and/or other heat source.
Monitor the depth of anesthesia continuously during surgery.
Increase the dosage of isoflurane when necessary.
Monitor the mouse carefully for response to external stimuli if using injectable anesthesia.
Redose the mouse appropriately using 25-33% of the initial dose of ketamine only if needed.
Proceed to step 9 for surgery on hairless mice.
Thoroughly shear the hair over the abdomen with an electric trimmer or shaver for hirsute mice.
Apply a 2-3 mm thick layer of hair removal cream over the shaved region using a cotton swabstick.
Leave the hair removal cream in place for 1-2 minutes.
Use sterile gauze to wipe off the cream towards the head, opposing the direction of the fur.
Remove any remaining cream with alcohol pads.
Immobilize the mouse for surgery.
Sterilize the surgical site with a Chlorhexidine swab stick.
Sterilize the surgical site with a 70% isopropyl alcohol wipe.
Perform a single ventral midline incision of 1.5 cm through the skin using sterile scissors, extending down from 5 mm above the base of the sternum.
Carefully disrupt the fascia located between the skin and underlying muscle by spreading the tips of spring scissors under the skin.
Apply 0.5% bupivacaine topically to the subcutaneous tissue for additional analgesia.
Make a 1 cm midline incision through the abdominal wall, taking care not to sever blood vessels.
Position the mouse on its back on a heated microscope stage.
Place a 4×4 inch rolled sterile gauze underneath the small of the back to better expose the liver.
Position the head to allow easy access for retro-orbital injection.
Restrain limbs using transpore surgical tape or other techniques.
Retract the skin and abdominal muscle.
Gently adjust the position of the incision with a cotton swab stick moistened with PBS, avoiding tugging on the liver or puncturing it.
Flush the liver with pre-warmed saline once properly positioned.
Place sterile gauze moistened with pre-warmed saline around the imaging site to prevent drying and imaging artifacts.
Place a disposable paper drape with a hole for imaging over the mouse to stabilize body temperature and maintain a sterile field.
Reduce the isoflurane concentration to between 0.8% and 1.2%, depending on the individual mouse.
Provide oxygen at a flow rate of 1.5L/min to avoid hypoxia.
Place an indwelling intraperitoneal line with a winged infusion set attached to a 1 ml syringe loaded with sterile PBS for experiments up to 12 hours.
Secure the indwelling intraperitoneal line with tape.
Supplement saline at a rate of 50 μl/h to compensate for fluid loss in multi-hour experiments.
Inject 50 μl saline hourly or administer fluids more frequently, such as 12.5 μl every 15 minutes.
Alternatively, administer fluids intravenously at a constant rate of 2-3ml/kg/h.
Disinfect a coverslip with sterile isopropyl alcohol swabs for liver imaging.
Position the coverslip in contact with the liver to maintain a sterile field and reduce tissue motion.
Bring the tissue into focus using a low magnification objective such as a 4×/NA 0.2 or 20×/NA 0.75 objective.
Take a high-quality image of the tissue using a white light or xenon/mercury light source.
Mark different regions on the reference image as they are imaged.
Switch to a high-resolution \(20× or 40× magnification\) objective without moving the mouse.
Select the appropriate excitation laser wavelengths \(640 nm for DiD, 488 nm for GFP, etc\).
Adjust tissue focus while monitoring the live image.
Monitor the flow of DiD-labeled red blood cells.
Monitor the mouse heart rate and breathing rate.
Adjust the concentration of isoflurane anesthesia to reduce motion during imaging.
Program the software to acquire images between appropriately spaced breaths for still images, if equipment allows.
Pre-program the microscope for automated image acquisition.
Set appropriate PMT gain and laser power for each contrast source.
Select FOVs for imaging.
Select appropriate scan speed, sampling interval, and imaging duration.
Acquire images at multiple magnifications using digital zoom.
Switch between Nyquist sampling and undersampling to capture data at inherent resolution of the system.
Identify landmarks that will predict where particles will accumulate.
Resuspend 5×10^8 nanoparticles in 60 μl PBS.
Sonicate the nanoparticles until monodisperse using a sonicating bath set to 37 °C.
Minimize the amount of free dye in the nanoparticle solution.
Load nanoparticles into a 28G ½ syringe.
Remove air from the syringe and cap it.
Dip the capped syringe several times vertically into the sonicating bath.
Inject nanoparticles retro-orbitally immediately after sonicating.
Sonicate the samples before loading into the syringe.
Sonicate the samples once they are in the syringe.
Inject the samples before particles settle.
Keep a sonicator near the animal imaging area.
Use proper needle capping technique to avoid injury.
Measure nanoparticle dispersity over time via dynamic light scattering if necessary.
Supplement unstable nanoparticle solutions with stabilizers prior to injection if needed.
Administer injections using the retro-orbital route for higher reproducibility and yield.
After injection, lubricate both eyes with a drop of ophthalmic ointment.
Begin imaging FOVs from the time of nanoparticle injection.
Use a frame-rate of 30 fps and a FOV of 250 × 250 μm for liver imaging.
Collect 1 – 3 min videos at each pre-programmed FOV to sample first-pass perfusion and early nanoparticle accumulation.
Avoid continuous imaging of a single region of interest to minimize laser-induced cytotoxicity.
Process each image as a multi-color overlay of all image acquisition channels using NIS elements or other image processing software.
Align frames based on vascular architecture visible in Tie2-GFP mice.
Choose the frames of interest for analysis after alignment.
Quantify frames within a single focal plane for tumor imaging applications.
Perform quantification over all video frames for liver accumulation studies.
Split each multi-color frame by acquisition channel/color to extract the nanoparticle channel.
Remove background noise such that individual nanoparticles can be clearly delineated.
Set a simple threshold if nanoparticles are sufficiently intense (high signal : noise ratio).
Utilize noise removal and/or object discrimination techniques if necessary for selecting nanoparticles.
Apply the same threshold for each frame within a video.
Create a binary mask to identify individual nanoparticles.
Set the mask to the maximum pixel value (255 for 8-bit images, 4095 for 12-bit images).
Apply the same mask to each frame.
Sum each frame with a later frame in the same video.
Set a new threshold above 255 (or 4095) to remove non-adherent particles.
Use object discrimination software to quantify the number of individual spots on a frame-by-frame basis.
Align and select frames as described in steps 24-25.
Split the frames by color to extract the nanoparticle channel.
Extract the Kupffer cell channel from the split frames.
Remove noise from each channel as described in steps 26-27.
Create a binary mask for each channel.
Apply an object discriminator to the cell channel if desired to remove RBCs based on circularity.
Set the mask pixel value to 255 and apply it to each frame.
Sum the two image channels for each frame.
Set a new threshold above 255 (or 4095) to remove particles that have not been internalized.
Use object discrimination software to quantify the total number of particles in each frame.
If particles appear to coalesce into fewer, larger particles upon internalization, adjust the object discrimination based on particle spot size, circularity, and/or intensity.
Experimentally determine the average spot size for singlet, doublet, triplet, etc. particles.
Use these measurements for accurate analyses to avoid underestimating the number of internalized particles.
Check the flow of DiD-labeled RBCs by scanning the tissue at 30 fps.
Compare this to a bright-field image of the same FOV to ensure that the tumor vasculature was not collapsed during coverslip placement.
Use the RBC flow to select the appropriate FOVs and focal planes for automated image acquisition.
Focus and identify the overall region-of-interest using a 4× objective (3.2×3.2 mm).
Sample all vascularized FOVs within the field at 3× digital zoom.
Prepare subcutaneous tumors for high-speed intravital microscopy.
Mount tumors such that they are sufficiently separated from the muscle fascia.
Perform line averaging of cropped images to reduce noise and improve image quality.
Scan images at 60 fps with 4 – 8× line averaging.
Image multiple FOVs (10-25 recommended) in parallel by preprogramming each FOV.
Cycle through each position twice per minute during imaging.
Acquire multiple frames at each position for up to 1 second.
Sample each position at 30-60 second intervals to yield kinetic curves describing particle influx and accumulation.
Program nanoparticle acquisition parameters using settings from a previous experiment or positive control.
Set up the microscope to sample multiple fields of view (FOVs) in parallel starting from the time of nanoparticle injection.
Acquire images continuously for one second at each FOV before moving to the next FOV.
Repeat the cycle every 30 seconds when approximately 25 FOVs are pre-programmed, yielding 7 frames/FOV/cycle.
Select the best frame per FOV/cycle for quantification purposes.
Adapt image magnification and scanning frame rates based on specific hardware availability.
Perform tumor imaging at lower magnification to increase the probability of detecting significant numbers of particles.
Use a 20 – 25× objective commonly used for intravital microscopy (IVM).
Apply digital zoom to achieve magnifications upwards of 60×, sufficient for most nanoparticle detection.
Acquire images at scanning rates adequate for capturing nanoparticle accumulation kinetics but not too slow for imaging RBC or particle trajectories if needed.
For trajectory measurements in the liver, sample FOVs at 30 – 60 fps for 10 – 30 second intervals.
